questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: A steady current of 3.2 A flows through a wire for 10 s. The number of electrons crossing a cross-section of the wire in this time is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C):

hints.text: Count charge crossing the section.
Use I = Q/t, then n = Q/e.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Keep seconds and coulombs consistent.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Count charge crossing the section.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use I = Q/t, then n = Q/e. Keep seconds and coulombs consistent.
3. Execution & Resolution: Current flows for 10 s, giving Q = 3.2×10 = 32 C; n = 32/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) = 2×10²⁰ electrons.
questions.check: Current flows for 10 s, giving Q = 3.2×10 = 32 C; n = 32/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) = 2×10²⁰ electrons.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: A device has a potential difference of 6 V across it. A total charge of 600 C passes through it in 2 minutes. The power consumed by the device is:

hints.text: Identify potential difference, transferred charge, and time.
Use electrical work W = VQ and P = W/t.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Convert two minutes into seconds.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Identify potential difference, transferred charge, and time.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use electrical work W = VQ and P = W/t. Convert two minutes into seconds.
3. Execution & Resolution: W = 6×600 = 3600 J over 120 s, so P = 30 W.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem:
The current through a wire varies with time as shown in Fig. 1. The total charge that flows through the wire in 15 s is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Current–time graph: current increases linearly from 0 A at 0 s to 4 A at 5 s, stays at 4 A until 10 s, and decreases linearly to 0 A at 15 s.

hints.text: Interpret current as charge transferred per second.
Charge equals the area under the I–t graph.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Split the graph into two triangles and one rectangle.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Interpret current as charge transferred per second.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Charge equals the area under the I–t graph. Split the graph into two triangles and one rectangle.
3. Execution & Resolution: Area = ½(5)(4) + (5)(4) + ½(5)(4) = 10+20+10 = 40 C.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about conduction in a metallic wire carrying a steady current is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: The drift speed of the free electrons is very small, of the order of mm/s.
B: The electric field that drives the current is set up in the wire almost at the speed of light.
C: The number of electrons crossing every cross-section per second is the same, even if the wire has non-uniform thickness.
D: Each free electron moves along the wire at constant speed without collisions.
questions.answer: A, B, C: The drift speed of the free electrons is very small, of the order of mm/s. | The electric field that drives the current is set up in the wire almost at the speed of light. | The number of electrons crossing every cross-section per second is the same, even if the wire has non-uniform thickness.

hints.text: Distinguish charge-carrier drift from signal propagation.
Use steady-state continuity and the collision model of a metal.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Evaluate each statement separately; multiple selections are allowed.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Distinguish charge-carrier drift from signal propagation.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use steady-state continuity and the collision model of a metal. Evaluate each statement separately; multiple selections are allowed.
3. Execution & Resolution: A is consistent with slow electron drift; B with rapid electromagnetic signal establishment; C with steady conservation of charge; D is false because carriers scatter.
questions.check: A is consistent with slow electron drift; B with rapid electromagnetic signal establishment; C with steady conservation of charge; D is false because carriers scatter.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: A steady current flows through a wire whose thicker part has three times the cross sectional area of its thinner part. The ratio of the drift speed of electrons in the thinner part to that in the thicker part is:

hints.text: Focus on the same series current in two portions of wire.
For a given material I = n e A v_d.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compare drift speeds inversely with cross-sectional area.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Focus on the same series current in two portions of wire.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For a given material I = n e A v_d. Compare drift speeds inversely with cross-sectional area.
3. Execution & Resolution: For the same I and n, v_thin/v_thick = A_thick/A_thin = 3.
questions.check: For the same I and n, v_thin/v_thick = A_thick/A_thin = 3.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: At a junction in a circuit, currents of 5 A and 3 A flow into the junction. Two wires carry 2 A and 4 A away from the junction. A fifth wire is also connected to the junction. The current in it is:
options: A: 2 A, flowing towards the junction
B: 6 A, flowing away from the junction
C: 2 A, flowing away from the junction
D: 6 A, flowing towards the junction
questions.answer: C: 2 A, flowing away from the junction

hints.text: Account for every current entering and leaving the junction.
Use Kirchhoff's current law: sum in = sum out.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compare 5+3 A entering against 2+4 A leaving.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Account for every current entering and leaving the junction.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use Kirchhoff's current law: sum in = sum out. Compare 5+3 A entering against 2+4 A leaving.
3. Execution & Resolution: 8 A enters in two wires; 6 A leaves in two, so 2 A must leave through the fifth.
questions.check: 8 A enters in two wires; 6 A leaves in two, so 2 A must leave through the fifth.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: The resistance of a wire is 10 Ω. It is uniformly stretched to twice its original length (its volume remains the same). The new resistance is:

hints.text: A stretched wire changes length and area.
Keep volume AL constant; R = ρL/A.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Express the new area in terms of the original area.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A stretched wire changes length and area.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Keep volume AL constant; R = ρL/A. Express the new area in terms of the original area.
3. Execution & Resolution: Length doubles, area halves, and R rises by a factor of four: 10 Ω→40 Ω.
questions.check: Length doubles, area halves, and R rises by a factor of four: 10 Ω→40 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: A wire of resistance 64 Ω is cut into four equal pieces, and the four pieces are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:

hints.text: Distinguish resistance of each cut piece from the original wire.
Resistance is proportional to length, then combine four equal pieces in parallel.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Cutting changes each resistance before the parallel connection.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Distinguish resistance of each cut piece from the original wire.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Resistance is proportional to length, then combine four equal pieces in parallel. Cutting changes each resistance before the parallel connection.
3. Execution & Resolution: Each quarter has 64/4=16 Ω; four identical 16 Ω pieces in parallel give 4 Ω.
questions.check: Each quarter has 64/4=16 Ω; four identical 16 Ω pieces in parallel give 4 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: Two wires of the same material have lengths in the ratio 1 : 2 and radii in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their resistances is:

hints.text: Compare both length and cross-sectional area.
For cylinders R ∝ L/r².

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Remember radius ratio is squared, not used directly.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Compare both length and cross-sectional area.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For cylinders R ∝ L/r². Remember radius ratio is squared, not used directly.
3. Execution & Resolution: R₁/R₂ = (1/2)×(2²/1²) = 2, giving 2:1.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem:
Fig. 2 shows the V–I graphs for two ohmic conductors A and B. The ratio of their resistances R_A : R_B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: V against I graph: straight lines A from (0,0) to (2 A,4 V) and B from (0,0) to (2 A,8 V).

hints.text: Read V–I axes: V vertical and I horizontal.
Resistance is the slope V/I for an ohmic line.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compare the two slopes at a shared current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Read V–I axes: V vertical and I horizontal.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Resistance is the slope V/I for an ohmic line. Compare the two slopes at a shared current.
3. Execution & Resolution: At 2 A, A reads 4 V and B 8 V; R_A:R_B = (4/2):(8/2) = 1:2.
questions.check: At 2 A, A reads 4 V and B 8 V; R_A:R_B = (4/2):(8/2) = 1:2.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem:
Fig. 3 shows the V–I graph of a filament lamp. Which of the following statements is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
[FIG-stem-1]
options: A: The increase in resistance is due to the rise in temperature of the filament.
B: The resistance of the filament increases as the current increases.
C: The lamp obeys Ohm's law over the whole range of current.
D: At every point the resistance of the lamp equals the slope of the graph at that point.
questions.answer: A, B: The increase in resistance is due to the rise in temperature of the filament. | The resistance of the filament increases as the current increases.
questions.figure_note: Nonlinear filament-lamp graph: V increases with I with an increasing slope; the graph passes approximately through (0,0) and (2 A,10 V).

hints.text: Observe the filament graph's changing slope.
Its static resistance is V/I, not generally the tangent slope dV/dI.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Temperature changes resistance during heating.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Observe the filament graph's changing slope.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Its static resistance is V/I, not generally the tangent slope dV/dI. Temperature changes resistance during heating.
3. Execution & Resolution: For a heated filament, A and B hold; C falsely assumes constant resistance, and D confuses V/I with differential resistance.
questions.check: For a heated filament, A and B hold; C falsely assumes constant resistance, and D confuses V/I with differential resistance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: The resistivity of a semiconductor increases when its temperature rises.
B: The resistivity of a metal increases when its temperature rises.
C: Manganin is used for making standard resistors because its resistivity changes very little with temperature.
D: Alloys generally have greater resistivity than the pure metals from which they are made.
questions.answer: B, C, D: The resistivity of a metal increases when its temperature rises. | Manganin is used for making standard resistors because its resistivity changes very little with temperature. | Alloys generally have greater resistivity than the pure metals from which they are made.

hints.text: Separate temperature behavior of metals and semiconductors.
Typical metallic resistivity increases with temperature; manganin varies little.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Treat each claim as an independent physical material statement.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Separate temperature behavior of metals and semiconductors.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Typical metallic resistivity increases with temperature; manganin varies little. Treat each claim as an independent physical material statement.
3. Execution & Resolution: B, C and D reflect common metal/alloy behavior; A is false for the usual semiconductor behavior.
questions.check: B, C and D reflect common metal/alloy behavior; A is false for the usual semiconductor behavior.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem:
A uniform wire of total resistance 12 Ω is bent into a circular ring. Two points P and Q on the ring are separated by an arc subtending 120° at the centre, as shown in Fig. 4. The resistance between P and Q is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Uniform 12-ohm ring with points P and Q separated by a 120-degree central arc.

hints.text: A ring provides two routes between P and Q.
Resistance is proportional to arc length, and the arcs are in parallel.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Split 360° into arcs of 120° and 240°.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A ring provides two routes between P and Q.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Resistance is proportional to arc length, and the arcs are in parallel. Split 360° into arcs of 120° and 240°.
3. Execution & Resolution: Two arcs have 4 Ω and 8 Ω; parallel equivalent = (4×8)/(4+8) = 8/3 Ω.
questions.check: Two arcs have 4 Ω and 8 Ω; parallel equivalent = (4×8)/(4+8) = 8/3 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: When a wire is uniformly stretched so that its length increases by 10% (its volume remaining constant), the percentage increase in its resistance is nearly:

hints.text: Conserving wire volume changes cross-section.
For same material and volume, R ∝ L².

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Increase length by factor 1.1 before squaring.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Conserving wire volume changes cross-section.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For same material and volume, R ∝ L². Increase length by factor 1.1 before squaring.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_new/R_old = 1.1² = 1.21, or 21% more.
questions.check: R_new/R_old = 1.1² = 1.21, or 21% more.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:

hints.text: Resistors share both terminals, so they are parallel.
Sum conductances, not resistances.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Resistors share both terminals, so they are parallel.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Sum conductances, not resistances. Use 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6.
3. Execution & Resolution: The conductance sum is 1 Ω⁻¹; R_eq = 1 Ω.
questions.check: The conductance sum is 1 Ω⁻¹; R_eq = 1 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 5, the cell has negligible internal resistance. The current through the 6 Ω resistor is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: 12 V cell in series with 4-ohm resistor, followed by 6-ohm and 3-ohm resistors in parallel.

hints.text: Locate true parallel nodes after the series resistor.
Reduce the 6 Ω and 3 Ω parallel pair before applying Ohm's law.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Calculate voltage across the parallel network.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Locate true parallel nodes after the series resistor.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Reduce the 6 Ω and 3 Ω parallel pair before applying Ohm's law. Calculate voltage across the parallel network.
3. Execution & Resolution: 6||3 = 2 Ω, total 4+2=6 Ω, source current 2 A, branch voltage 4 V, current through 6 Ω = 2/3 A.
questions.check: 6||3 = 2 Ω, total 4+2=6 Ω, source current 2 A, branch voltage 4 V, current through 6 Ω = 2/3 A.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem: The ratio of the equivalent resistance of five identical resistors connected in series to that when they are connected in parallel is:

hints.text: Keep the number of identical resistors fixed.
For n identical R: series=nR, parallel=R/n.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Take the ratio after finding both equivalents.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Keep the number of identical resistors fixed.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For n identical R: series=nR, parallel=R/n. Take the ratio after finding both equivalents.
3. Execution & Resolution: Five in series = 5R, five in parallel = R/5; ratio 25:1.
questions.check: Five in series = 5R, five in parallel = R/5; ratio 25:1.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
The equivalent resistance between A and B in the network of Fig. 6 is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Diamond bridge: AC 2 ohms, CB 4 ohms, AD 3 ohms, DB 6 ohms and CD 5 ohms; terminals A and B.

hints.text: Read the bridge node labels and resistor values.
Check whether the Wheatstone bridge is balanced.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: If intermediate potentials are equal, the central resistor carries no current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Read the bridge node labels and resistor values.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Check whether the Wheatstone bridge is balanced. If intermediate potentials are equal, the central resistor carries no current.
3. Execution & Resolution: 2/3 = 4/6 makes the bridge balanced. Remaining branches 2+4=6 Ω and 3+6=9 Ω in parallel give 3.6 Ω.
questions.check: 2/3 = 4/6 makes the bridge balanced. Remaining branches 2+4=6 Ω and 3+6=9 Ω in parallel give 3.6 Ω.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
Twelve identical resistors, each of 12 Ω, form the edges of a cube as shown in Fig. 7. The equivalent resistance between the opposite corners A and B of the body diagonal is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Twelve 12-ohm edges of a cube; A and B are opposite body-diagonal vertices.

hints.text: Identify the terminals as opposite vertices of the cube.
Use equipotential groupings for a uniform twelve-edge cube.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: The body diagonal differs from edge and face diagonals.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Identify the terminals as opposite vertices of the cube.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use equipotential groupings for a uniform twelve-edge cube. The body diagonal differs from edge and face diagonals.
3. Execution & Resolution: Standard symmetric nodal reduction gives R_body = (5/6)r, so with r=12 Ω the equivalent is 10 Ω; an independent nodal witness is still required for academic admission.
questions.check: Standard symmetric nodal reduction gives R_body = (5/6)r, so with r=12 Ω the equivalent is 10 Ω; an independent nodal witness is still required for academic admission.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem: Three resistors, each of resistance R, are connected to form a triangle ABC. The equivalent resistance between the corners A and B is:

hints.text: Trace direct and indirect paths in the triangle.
One branch is R; the other contains two series resistors.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: The two branches connect the same terminal pair.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Trace direct and indirect paths in the triangle.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: One branch is R; the other contains two series resistors. The two branches connect the same terminal pair.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_eq = R||(2R) = (2R²)/(3R)=2R/3.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 8, the cell has negligible internal resistance. The current through the 2 Ω resistor is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: 6 V cell across parallel branches, one branch 4 ohms and 2 ohms in series and the other 3 ohms.

hints.text: Trace each branch from the top rail to the bottom rail.
The 4 Ω and 2 Ω resistors share an uninterrupted branch.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Use the branch potential of the ideal 6 V cell.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Trace each branch from the top rail to the bottom rail.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: The 4 Ω and 2 Ω resistors share an uninterrupted branch. Use the branch potential of the ideal 6 V cell.
3. Execution & Resolution: Series branch 4+2=6 Ω receives 6 V, so its current and the 2 Ω resistor's current is 1 A.
questions.check: Series branch 4+2=6 Ω receives 6 V, so its current and the 2 Ω resistor's current is 1 A.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 9, the cell has negligible internal resistance. When the switch S is closed (compared with S open), which of the following is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
[FIG-stem-1]
options: A: The power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor becomes zero.
B: The total power supplied by the cell decreases.
C: The current from the cell increases from 1 A to 3 A.
D: The potential difference across the 2 Ω resistor doubles.
questions.answer: A, C: The power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor becomes zero. | The current from the cell increases from 1 A to 3 A.
questions.figure_note: 6 V cell with 2-ohm and 4-ohm series resistors, and a switch bypassing the 4-ohm resistor.

hints.text: Compare circuits with the switch open and closed.
When closed, the ideal switch bypasses the 4 Ω element.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compute source currents in both states.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Compare circuits with the switch open and closed.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: When closed, the ideal switch bypasses the 4 Ω element. Compute source currents in both states.
3. Execution & Resolution: Open: (2+4)=6 Ω, I=1 A. Closed: 2 Ω, I=3 A, no 4 Ω power. Statements A and C hold.
questions.check: Open: (2+4)=6 Ω, I=1 A. Closed: 2 Ω, I=3 A, no 4 Ω power. Statements A and C hold.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: A heater coil of resistance 20 Ω carries a current of 3 A for 5 minutes. The heat produced is:

hints.text: Use the heater's resistance, current and duration.
Joule heat is Q = I²Rt.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Convert five minutes to seconds.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Use the heater's resistance, current and duration.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Joule heat is Q = I²Rt. Convert five minutes to seconds.
3. Execution & Resolution: Q = 3²×20×300 = 54,000 J = 54 kJ.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: Two electric bulbs rated 60 W and 100 W, both for 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Which statement is correct?
options: A: The 100 W bulb glows brighter than the 60 W bulb
C: Both glow with their rated power
D: The 60 W bulb glows brighter than the 100 W bulb
questions.answer: D: The 60 W bulb glows brighter than the 100 W bulb

hints.text: Bulb rating determines nominal resistance.
At the same rated voltage R=V²/P.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: The bulbs in series carry the same current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Bulb rating determines nominal resistance.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: At the same rated voltage R=V²/P. The bulbs in series carry the same current.
3. Execution & Resolution: The 60 W bulb has larger nominal R and hence greater I²R heating, so D under the rated-resistance approximation; thermal nonlinearity is an academic caveat.
questions.check: The 60 W bulb has larger nominal R and hence greater I²R heating, so D under the rated-resistance approximation; thermal nonlinearity is an academic caveat.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: Two bulbs of 100 W and 25 W, both rated for 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. The potential difference across the 100 W bulb is:

hints.text: Convert rated powers to nominal resistances.
At the same 220 V rating, R∝1/P.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Divide series voltage in proportion to R.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Convert rated powers to nominal resistances.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: At the same 220 V rating, R∝1/P. Divide series voltage in proportion to R.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_100:R_25=1:4; the 100 W bulb gets 220/(1+4)=44 V under nominal-R approximation.
questions.check: R_100:R_25=1:4; the 100 W bulb gets 220/(1+4)=44 V under nominal-R approximation.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: Four bulbs of 60 W each are used for 5 hours every day for 30 days. If electrical energy costs ₹ 6 per unit (kWh), the bill for the month is:

hints.text: Calculate total electrical power before multiplying by hours.
Cost is energy in kWh times tariff.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Convert 4×60 W into kW, then multiply by days.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Calculate total electrical power before multiplying by hours.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Cost is energy in kWh times tariff. Convert 4×60 W into kW, then multiply by days.
3. Execution & Resolution: Power = 0.24 kW; time = 150 h; energy = 36 kWh; cost = ₹216.
questions.check: Power = 0.24 kW; time = 150 h; energy = 36 kWh; cost = ₹216.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: An electric heater is rated 2 kW, 220 V. Which of the following fuse ratings is most suitable for its circuit?

hints.text: Calculate normal working current from rating.
Use I=P/V, then select a suitable listed protective fuse.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compare candidate fuse ratings with approximately 9.1 A.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Calculate normal working current from rating.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use I=P/V, then select a suitable listed protective fuse. Compare candidate fuse ratings with approximately 9.1 A.
3. Execution & Resolution: Operating current ≈ 2000/220 = 9.09 A; the worksheet chooses 10 A. Real fuse design also requires rating and inrush considerations.
questions.check: Operating current ≈ 2000/220 = 9.09 A; the worksheet chooses 10 A. Real fuse design also requires rating and inrush considerations.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: A heater coil dissipates 1 kW when connected to a mains supply. A piece equal to 1/4 of its length is cut off and the remaining coil is connected to the same supply. The power dissipated is:

hints.text: Removing length changes resistance at fixed voltage.
For same wire material/cross section R∝L, and P=V²/R.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Remaining length is three-quarters of the original.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Removing length changes resistance at fixed voltage.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For same wire material/cross section R∝L, and P=V²/R. Remaining length is three-quarters of the original.
3. Execution & Resolution: R' = 3R/4; P' = P×4/3 = 4/3 kW.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: A 1 kW immersion heater has an efficiency of 80%. The time it takes to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C is (specific heat of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹):

hints.text: Convert temperature rise into heat delivered to water.
Use Q=mcΔT and efficiency η=Q/(P_in t).

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Power delivered to water is 0.8×1 kW.

questions.stem: A cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to an external resistance of 5 Ω. The potential difference across the terminals of the cell is:

hints.text: Internal resistance reduces terminal potential.
Use I=ℰ/(R+r), then V_terminal=IR.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Compute the current with both resistances included.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Internal resistance reduces terminal potential.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use I=ℰ/(R+r), then V_terminal=IR. Compute the current with both resistances included.
3. Execution & Resolution: I=6/(5+1)=1 A and V_terminal=1×5=5 V.
questions.check: I=6/(5+1)=1 A and V_terminal=1×5=5 V.

questions.stem: Three identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series with an external resistor of 4.5 Ω. The current in the resistor is:

hints.text: Cells in series add both emf and internal resistance.
Use I=Σℰ/(R+Σr).

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Do not omit any cell's 0.5 Ω internal resistance.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Cells in series add both emf and internal resistance.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Use I=Σℰ/(R+Σr). Do not omit any cell's 0.5 Ω internal resistance.
3. Execution & Resolution: Total emf 6 V; total resistance 4.5+1.5=6 Ω; I=1 A.
questions.check: Total emf 6 V; total resistance 4.5+1.5=6 Ω; I=1 A.

questions.subject: PHYSICS
questions.subtopic: Cells, Internal Resistance and Measuring Instruments
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about electrical meters is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.
B: An ideal ammeter has infinite resistance.
C: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component whose potential difference is to be measured.
D: An ammeter is connected in series with the part of the circuit whose current is to be measured.
questions.answer: A, C, D: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance. | A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component whose potential difference is to be measured. | An ammeter is connected in series with the part of the circuit whose current is to be measured.

hints.text: Ideal meters have different limits.
An ideal voltmeter draws zero current; an ideal ammeter adds zero resistance.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Check each connection statement separately.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Ideal meters have different limits.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: An ideal voltmeter draws zero current; an ideal ammeter adds zero resistance. Check each connection statement separately.
3. Execution & Resolution: A true (infinite voltmeter resistance); B false; C true (parallel voltmeter); D true (series ammeter).
questions.check: A true (infinite voltmeter resistance); B false; C true (parallel voltmeter); D true (series ammeter).

[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: 9 V cell with 6-ohm and 3-ohm series resistors, ideal voltmeter connected across the 3-ohm resistor.

hints.text: The voltmeter has infinite resistance in the ideal limit.
The 6 Ω and 3 Ω series resistors divide the 9 V source.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Measure across the 3 Ω component without loading it.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The voltmeter has infinite resistance in the ideal limit.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: The 6 Ω and 3 Ω series resistors divide the 9 V source. Measure across the 3 Ω component without loading it.
3. Execution & Resolution: I=9/(6+3)=1 A; V_3Ω=3 V.

questions.stem: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection for a current of 5 mA. To convert it into a voltmeter of range 0 to 10 V, a resistance must be connected:

For a voltmeter, add series resistance R_s = V/I_g − R_g.

questions.stem:
A cell is connected to a variable resistor. The terminal potential difference V of the cell is plotted against the current I drawn from it in Fig. 11. The emf and the internal resistance of the cell are:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Straight terminal-voltage versus current plot from (0 A,6 V) to (3 A,0 V), with a marked point (2 A,2 V).

hints.text: Read the intercept and slope of the terminal-voltage graph.
For a cell, V = ℰ − I r.

hints.prompt: Tier 3 — Plan a check without the answer
hints.text: Intercept gives ℰ; slope magnitude gives r.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Read the intercept and slope of the terminal-voltage graph.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: For a cell, V = ℰ − I r. Intercept gives ℰ; slope magnitude gives r.
3. Execution & Resolution: At I=0, V=6 V; at I=3 A, V=0; r=−ΔV/ΔI=2 Ω.
questions.check: At I=0, V=6 V; at I=3 A, V=0; r=−ΔV/ΔI=2 Ω.
